summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as recorded on 12 March 2026. Legal gender recognition is not available, and no legislation recognises LGBTI people or protects gender identity, so a trans visitor's documents will be read exactly as issued and cannot be aligned with lived gender.

Organisational recognition is closed. The registrar of companies refused registration to an LGBTI group in July 2019, and officials had already refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities in June 2019 on grounds of morality. In April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. A visitor should not expect to find a registered national advocacy body to contact for assistance.

Hostility from official figures is on the record. A 2021 United States State Department report found that some traditional, religious and government officials publicly criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini stated that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider it; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a United Nations working group call for an LGBTQ protection law on the basis that too few gay people lived in Eswatini to justify drafting one, and in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures protecting people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public visibility nonetheless exists and has been tolerated on specific occasions. The first Eswatini Pride was held in July 2018 and declared a success, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident. A church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018, documented alongside an absence of let-up in discrimination.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced.

Healthcare access is documented as unreliable for gender-diverse and gay visitors and residents alike. A 2019 survey found that 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, and 30% had been denied healthcare services. Public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign in February 2012 urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion.

Violence risk is evidenced locally. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a gay man had been murdered in the same town a few months earlier. Rock of Hope states that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. A 2013 survey found that 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal.

Protections exist in policy documents rather than in statute. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, the 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Eswatini Not Free in Freedom in the World 2024, with an overall score of 17/100, comprising 1/40 for political rights and 16/60 for civil liberties, describing an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment, in which 'Mswati must fall' had become a common protest slogan. Restrictions on LGBTI organisation therefore sit alongside restrictions on political organising generally rather than standing alone.

The gap between policy language and enforceable law is the central comparison for this jurisdiction: several national strategies, guidelines and broadcasting rules name sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds, while no statute provides a remedy for discrimination on those grounds.
localsOnly:
Residents live with a set of policy instruments that name them without granting legal standing. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) recognise equality as including freedom from discrimination based on sex or sexual orientation and identify LGBT people as a key population at elevated risk of gender-based violence; the National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 carries sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles; and the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation.

Health policy at national level is inclusive on its face. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health obliges the Ministry of Health to provide family planning information and services regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and the Health Ministry extended HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples in 2012, a step LGBTQ groups welcomed at the time.

Media regulation constrains hostile content. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines prohibit licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation.

Family law treats same-sex and different-sex couples unequally: same-sex couples may not adopt, whereas heterosexual prospective adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced, and no same-sex relationship is legally recognised.

Community-level inclusion is documented alongside continued discrimination. A church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018, and the first Eswatini Pride took place in July 2018, while Rock of Hope reports that most LGBTQ people remain in the closet or leave for South Africa.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not state the statutory penalty for same-sex relations in Eswatini, so no sentence, fine or term of imprisonment is asserted here; the offence's existence is sourced, its punishment is not.

No source in the inventory addresses entry procedures, visa decisions, border questioning or airport screening as they affect trans travellers, and none addresses the rules governing gender markers on Eswatini passports or other identity documents. Whether a visitor's documents are inspected at the border, and what follows, remains unresolved.

Enforcement is not documented. The inventory records no prosecution, arrest or acquittal under the sodomy or related provisions, so the frequency and selectivity of enforcement cannot be stated.

Several claims rest on a single encyclopedic compilation rather than primary or institutional sources, including the adoption prohibition, the 2019 health-facility survey figures, the 2013 suicide and substance-use figures, and the statements attributed to Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini, Percy Simelane and Mgwagwa Gamedze. These are carried as reported and are not independently corroborated here.

The evidence base is unevenly dated. The criminalisation and gender-recognition findings are current to 12 March 2026, but the surveys, court rulings and policy documents cited range from 2012 to 2024, and no source establishes whether the 2021 policy language has been implemented or funded.
